title: ⭐ Practice: initials, slices and one small word

questions.prompt: A charity page says that one dollar alone can provide eight children with pencils and exercise books. A pupil reading it pictures a shelf of books about sport. What are exercise books really?

options.text: the printed books a teacher sets for a subject
the books a school lends out from its library
the books in which a school records its pupils' marks
the blank books in which a pupil writes his own work

questions.explanation: The trap is in the first of the two words, which has nothing to do with physical training here: an exercise is a piece of work you are set, and the book that goes with it arrives empty and leaves full of your handwriting. That is also why a dollar can buy several of them at once and why they are named in the same breath as pencils - both are things a child uses up. A book already printed by somebody else, a book waiting on a library shelf, a book kept in an office with marks in it: each of those exists, each has its own name, and none of them is bought by the boxful for a dollar.

questions.prompt: Four international bodies, and all four names open on the very same word. Match each set of initials with the name behind it.

options.text: WHO
WFP
WTO
WWF
World Trade Organization
World Health Organization
World Wide Fund
World Food Programme

questions.explanation: One letter for one word, taken in order: that is the whole machine, and here it is the second letter that carries all the information, since the first is the same four times over. H opens health, F opens food, T opens trade, and a repeated W opens the adjective of a fund that calls itself worldwide. The third letter then confirms what you have: the programme, the organization, the fund. Work through the letters in order and none of the four can be mistaken for another, however alike they look on a page.

questions.prompt: One September a village school writes 240 children into its register. In the same village, eleven children of exactly that age are written into no register anywhere. Which pair of words names those two facts, in that order?

options.text: the enrolment of 240 children, and the exclusion of eleven
the exclusion of 240 children, and the enrolment of eleven
the enrolment of 240 children, and the attendance of eleven
the attendance of 240 children, and the exclusion of eleven

questions.explanation: Two hundred and forty names went down on a list, and that act of registration has its own noun. Eleven children of the same age did not get onto any list at all, and being kept outside the system in that way is what a report on children out of school is written to measure. Turn the pair round and you have a village that struck 240 children off and admitted eleven, which is not what happened. And the word for turning up day after day names something else entirely: it counts faces in a room in March, not names on a list in September, and no eleven children who are absent from every register can be counted by it.

questions.prompt: Before he looks at a single slice, a pupil is told to read the heading of a pie chart and the school year printed beside it. What do those few words settle for him?

options.text: which slice is the largest, and how far ahead of the others it stands
what quantity has been cut up, and the year the count belongs to
how many children of primary age there were in the world that year
why the children of the largest region were not going to school

questions.explanation: A slice is a share, and a share means nothing until you know what it is a share of. The heading names that whole - here, the children of primary age the world had left outside a classroom - and the two years beside it tie the count to one school year rather than to today. Everything else on the page rests on those two facts. How big the slices are is a matter for the slices; how many children were alive that year is a quantity this circle never shows; and causes are not drawn on charts at all, which is why a paragraph is printed beside one.

questions.prompt: A reading room puts a notice on its door: "Members will lose their key unless they bring the borrowing register back by the end of the month." Fatma brought the register back on the twelfth. What does the notice say about her key?

options.text: she loses it, since the notice says members will lose their keys
nothing is settled, since the notice covers only members who do not bring it
she keeps it, since bringing the register back is what saves it
she loses it, since a member has to bring the register back every month

questions.explanation: A sentence built on this word sets one condition and then settles both sides of it at once. The member who fails the condition loses the key; the member who meets it therefore keeps it, and that second half is said just as clearly, even though no line of the notice spells it out. Fatma met it on the twelfth, well inside the month. Reading only the threat and stopping there turns a conditional warning into a flat announcement that everybody is about to lose a key, which no reading room would ever pin up; and there is nothing in the notice about a register that has to travel back and forth month after month.

questions.prompt: A table of children out of school in 2001/02 has one column for the share of the world total and one for the number of children, the world total being 115 million. The line for Eastern and Southern Africa reads 21.4 million, and its share box has been left empty. Which figure belongs in it?
questions.explanation: The two columns hold the same fact in two units, so one can always be got from the other: 21.4 divided by 115 comes out a little under a fifth, which the table prints as 18.6 per cent. The tempting slip is to carry the head count straight across as though a number of children and a share of a total were the same kind of quantity - they are not, and 21.4 per cent of that world total would mean nearly 25 million children, three and a half million more than the line actually gives. The two smaller and larger shares on offer belong to other rows of the same table: one to the Pacific side of Asia, the other to South Asia, which alone carries more than a third of the world's total.
